deck.title: Lambda
deck.analogy: Lambda is a contractor who materializes on your doorstep when the doorbell rings, does one job, vanishes, and bills only for the time he existed.

cards.front: What is AWS Lambda and how is it billed?

back.answer: Serverless compute: upload a function, an event triggers it, and you pay per millisecond of execution.
back.explanation: AWS handles provisioning, scaling and patching. It scales automatically per event; no traffic means no cost.
back.mnemonic: Contractor appears at the doorbell, does one job, vanishes: code without a computer.

cards.front: Lambda: what is the maximum execution time?

back.answer: 15 minutes.
back.explanation: This is a hard ceiling and the source of many exam traps.

cards.sourceHeading: Hard limits — where half the traps live

cards.front: Lambda: what is the memory range and how does CPU relate?

back.answer: 128 MB to 10 GB; CPU scales with memory (no separate CPU setting).

cards.sourceHeading: Hard limits — where half the traps live

cards.front: Lambda: how large can ephemeral /tmp storage be?

back.answer: Up to 10 GB.

cards.sourceHeading: Hard limits — where half the traps live

cards.front: Lambda: deployment package size limits and container image limit?

back.answer: Zip: 50 MB zipped / 250 MB unzipped. Container image: up to 10 GB.

cards.sourceHeading: Hard limits — where half the traps live

cards.front: Lambda: default concurrency per region?

back.answer: 1,000 (raisable).

cards.sourceHeading: Hard limits — where half the traps live

cards.front: A 2-hour video processing job: can Lambda run it?

back.answer: No — 15-minute ceiling. Use AWS Batch or ECS/Fargate.
back.explanation: Step Functions is right only if the work can be divided into chunks under 15 minutes each.

cards.sourceHeading: Hard limits — where half the traps live

cards.front: A CPU-bound Lambda function is slow. How do you speed it up?

back.answer: Increase the memory; CPU scales with memory.
back.explanation: There is no CPU setting. It reads like a wrong answer but is the right one.

cards.sourceHeading: Hard limits — where half the traps live

cards.front: Lambda synchronous invocation: how does it work?

back.answer: The caller waits for the result; errors go straight back to the caller. Classic: API Gateway → Lambda.
back.mnemonic: Hand-delivered mail: you wait for the reply.

cards.sourceHeading: Three ways a Lambda gets invoked

cards.front: Lambda asynchronous invocation: how does it work and on failure?

back.answer: Source (S3, SNS, EventBridge) pushes the event and leaves; Lambda queues it and retries twice on failure.
back.explanation: After the retries the event is gone unless a DLQ or failure destination is configured.

cards.sourceHeading: Three ways a Lambda gets invoked

cards.front: Asynchronously invoked Lambda events are lost on failure. Fix?

back.answer: Add a DLQ or on-failure destination.
back.explanation: Async retries twice, then drops the event.

cards.sourceHeading: Three ways a Lambda gets invoked

cards.front: Lambda Event Source Mapping: which sources and how does it work?

back.answer: For SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, Lambda polls (pulls) and processes records in batches.
back.explanation: Failed batches return to the queue and eventually reach the queue's own DLQ.
back.mnemonic: PO box: you walk to collect. Knockers (S3/SNS/EventBridge) vs buckets to visit (SQS/Kinesis/Streams).

cards.sourceHeading: Three ways a Lambda gets invoked

cards.front: What is a Lambda cold start?

back.answer: The pause on first invocation after idle while AWS loads runtime and code.
back.explanation: Appears as sporadic latency spikes after periods of inactivity.

cards.front: Lambda Provisioned vs Reserved Concurrency?

back.answer: Provisioned = Pre-warmed instances that kill cold starts; Reserved = Restricted cap protecting downstream systems.
back.explanation: Reserved example: a fragile legacy database that dies past 50 connections.

cards.front: What happens when you put Lambda in a VPC?

back.answer: It gets an ENI in your subnet and can reach private RDS, but loses internet access.
back.explanation: Default Lambda runs outside the VPC with internet but no private resources. Restore internet with NAT Gateway (or VPC endpoints for AWS services).

cards.front: Why use RDS Proxy with Lambda?

back.answer: Many short-lived functions each opening DB connections exhaust the database; RDS Proxy pools and shares connections.
back.explanation: Lambda + RDS in the same sentence → RDS Proxy.

cards.front: Lambda execution role: what is it?

back.answer: The IAM role attached to the function; it is the function's permissions.
back.explanation: "Lambda can't write to DynamoDB" → fix the execution role.

cards.sourceHeading: Odds and ends the exam sprinkles in

cards.front: Lambda Layers: purpose?

back.answer: Package shared libraries/dependencies once and reuse across functions.

cards.sourceHeading: Odds and ends the exam sprinkles in

cards.front: Lambda dependencies exceed the 250 MB zip limit. Solution?

back.answer: Deploy as a container image, up to 10 GB.

cards.sourceHeading: Odds and ends the exam sprinkles in

cards.front: Lambda environment variables: use and secret protection?

back.answer: Config kept outside code; encrypt secrets with KMS.

cards.sourceHeading: Odds and ends the exam sprinkles in

cards.front: How do you run a task every night at 2 AM without servers using Lambda?

back.answer: EventBridge scheduled rule → Lambda (serverless cron).

cards.sourceHeading: Odds and ends the exam sprinkles in

cards.front: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions: runtime?

back.answer: Lambda@Edge: Node.js/Python, up to seconds. CloudFront Functions: JavaScript only, sub-millisecond.

cards.sourceHeading: Code at the edge: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions

cards.front: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions: network calls?

back.answer: Lambda@Edge: yes. CloudFront Functions: no.

cards.sourceHeading: Code at the edge: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions

cards.front: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions: hooks?

back.answer: Lambda@Edge: viewer + origin request/response. CloudFront Functions: viewer request/response only.

cards.sourceHeading: Code at the edge: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions

cards.front: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions: cost?

back.answer: Lambda@Edge is baseline; CloudFront Functions is about 1/6 the price.

cards.sourceHeading: Code at the edge: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions

cards.front: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions: typical use?

back.answer: Lambda@Edge: JWT/auth validation, origin selection, real logic. CloudFront Functions: header manipulation, URL rewrites/redirects.
back.explanation: External calls or real logic → Lambda@Edge; trivial tweak on every request → CloudFront Functions.

cards.sourceHeading: Code at the edge: Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions

cards.front: A 90-minute video transcoding job. Can it run on Lambda?

back.answer: No — AWS Batch / Fargate (15-minute hard limit).
back.explanation: Step Functions only if divisible into <15-min steps.

choices.why: Removes cold starts, not the time limit.

cards.front: Generate a thumbnail whenever an image lands in S3. Design?

back.answer: S3 event notification → Lambda (canonical async trigger).

choices.why: Edge functions don't react to S3 uploads.

cards.front: Lambda-backed API is fast normally but has latency spikes after idle periods. Fix?

back.answer: Provisioned Concurrency (Pre-warmed, no cold starts).

choices.why: Keeps instances warm, eliminating cold starts.

cards.front: Lambda scaling overwhelms a legacy database that handles only 50 connections. Fix?

back.answer: Reserved Concurrency cap (Restricted), plus RDS Proxy.

choices.why: Limits parallel copies to protect the database.

cards.front: Lambda must query an RDS database in a private subnet. Solution?

back.answer: Attach Lambda to the VPC + RDS Proxy (add NAT if it still needs internet).

choices.text: Attach Lambda to VPC + RDS Proxy

cards.front: A CPU-intensive Lambda function is too slow. What do you do?

back.answer: Increase memory (CPU scales with memory).

choices.why: More memory gives proportionally more CPU.

cards.front: Run a cleanup script every night at 2 AM with no servers. Design?

back.answer: EventBridge schedule → Lambda (serverless cron).

cards.front: Validate JWT tokens / call an external auth service at the edge. Which?

back.answer: Lambda@Edge (network calls allowed; CloudFront Functions can't).

choices.why: Supports network calls and real logic.

cards.front: Rewrite URLs or add security headers on millions of requests, cheapest. Which?

back.answer: CloudFront Functions (sub-ms, ~1/6 price, no network).

choices.why: Costlier than needed for trivial tweaks.

cards.front: An asynchronously invoked Lambda fails and events disappear. Fix?

back.answer: DLQ / on-failure destination (async retries twice, then drops).

choices.why: Changes the architecture; doesn't preserve events.
Captures events after retries are exhausted.

cards.front: Lambda should process SQS messages. Mechanism?

back.answer: Event Source Mapping (Lambda pulls in batches; failures return to the queue).

choices.why: Lambda polls SQS and batches records.

cards.front: Keyword: **"Job > 15 minutes"**

back.answer: NOT Lambda → Batch / Fargate

cards.front: Keyword: **"Divisible into <15-min steps"**

back.answer: Step Functions

cards.front: Keyword: **"CPU-bound slow function"**

back.answer: Increase memory

cards.front: Keyword: **"Cold start latency"**

back.answer: Provisioned Concurrency (Pre-warmed)

cards.front: Keyword: **"Protect downstream / cap invocations"**

back.answer: Reserved Concurrency (Restricted)

cards.front: Keyword: **"Lambda + RDS"**

back.answer: RDS Proxy (+ VPC config)

cards.front: Keyword: **"VPC Lambda lost internet"**

back.answer: NAT Gateway / VPC endpoints

cards.front: Keyword: **"Async failures lost"**

back.answer: DLQ / failure destination

cards.front: Keyword: **"SQS / Kinesis / DDB Streams"**

back.answer: Event Source Mapping (pull, batches)

cards.front: Keyword: **"S3 / SNS / EventBridge"**

back.answer: Async push (2 retries)

cards.front: Keyword: **"Serverless cron"**

back.answer: EventBridge schedule → Lambda

cards.front: Keyword: **"Shared dependencies"**

back.answer: Layers

cards.front: Keyword: **"Deps > 250 MB"**

back.answer: Container image (10 GB)

cards.front: Keyword: **"Function permissions"**

back.answer: Execution role

cards.front: Keyword: **"Edge + network calls / JWT"**

back.answer: Lambda@Edge

cards.front: Keyword: **"Edge header/URL tweak, cheapest"**

back.answer: CloudFront Functions

cards.front: Keyword: **"Max runtime / memory / concurrency"**

back.answer: 15 min / 10 GB / 1,000 default
